subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Trust Game
description: A 60-second lesson on The Trust Game.

hook.text: You give a stranger $10. It triples to $30. The stranger can keep it all or share. Most strangers share.

buildup.text: Berg's trust game measures how much people trust anonymous partners. Economists expected zero trust. They were wrong.

discovery.text: On average, senders gave half their money and receivers returned slightly more.

twist.text: Oxytocin increases trust. Zak found that people given oxytocin sent 17% more money.

climax.text: Trust reduces transaction costs in economies. High-trust societies have stronger markets and faster growth.

punchline.text: Trust is not naive. It is economic infrastructure.

quiz.question: What did Berg's trust game reveal?
options: People trust and cooperate more than economic models predict
Trust depends entirely on the amount of money involved

details.summary: In the trust game, one player sends money to another player, the amount is multiplied, and the second player decides how much to return. Most people send money despite the risk of betrayal, and most recipients return a fair share, demonstrating baseline human trust.
details.whyItMatters: The trust game quantifies the foundation of economic exchange: willingness to be vulnerable. Societies with higher trust levels in these experiments also have higher GDP, lower transaction costs, and stronger economic institutions.
takeaways: Most people trust strangers with real money in experimental settings
Trust levels in the lab correlate with national economic performance
Oxytocin and institutional quality both enhance trusting behavior

faq.question: How much do people typically trust in the trust game?
faq.answer: On average, senders transfer about 50 percent of their endowment, and recipients return about 50 percent of the tripled amount. This means trust is generally rewarded, which sustains the behavior. Complete betrayal is relatively uncommon.

faq.question: Why does oxytocin increase trust in experiments?
faq.answer: Intranasal oxytocin increases the amount people send in trust games by reducing the fear of betrayal. This biological mechanism suggests that trust has deep neurochemical roots and is not purely a calculated risk assessment.
